title: Hierarchical Clustering & Dendrograms

blocks.t: From the notes
Hierarchical clustering, as written
Two kinds:

items:
Agglomerative — bottom up. Every point starts as its
own cluster; we keep merging the two closest clusters until
only one is left.

Divisive — top down. Start with one big cluster and keep
splitting.

blocks.t:
The picture of the merges is called a dendrogram. The
height of a join is the distance at which those two clusters
merged.

We do not need to give k in advance — we cut the dendrogram
horizontally, and the number of vertical lines it crosses is the number of
clusters.

Distance between two clusters is decided by the linkage:
single (minimum), complete (maximum), average,
ward.

blocks.t: The algorithm
Agglomerative clustering (AGNES):

items: Start with $n$ clusters, one per point.
Compute the $n\times n$ pairwise distance matrix.

Find the two closest clusters $A,B$ and merge them. Record the merge
height $d(A,B)$.

Update the distances from the new cluster $A\cup B$ to all others, using
the linkage rule.
Repeat from 3 until one cluster remains.

blocks.t: This produces exactly $n-1$ merges, and the full history is the dendrogram.

Step 4 does not require re-scanning the raw data: all four standard linkages
obey the Lance–Williams recurrence
d(A\cup B, C)=\alpha_A d(A,C)+\alpha_B d(B,C)+\beta d(A,B)+\gamma |d(A,C)-d(B,C)|,

with constants that depend only on the linkage and the cluster sizes. That is
why the whole procedure runs on the distance matrix alone.

Divisive clustering (DIANA) is the mirror image, but it is rarely
used: at the first step it must consider $2^{n-1}-1$ possible splits of the
whole dataset. Practical implementations approximate it (e.g. bisecting
K-Means). Agglomerative is what people mean by "hierarchical clustering".
The four linkages — and why the choice matters most

blocks.t:
Ward's criterion deserves the detail. It merges the pair whose union
increases the total within-cluster sum of squares by the least. That increase
has a closed form:
\Delta(A,B) = \frac{|A| |B|}{|A|+|B|} \big\|\mu_A-\mu_B\big\|^2 .

Note the size factor: merging two large clusters is penalised even when
their centres are close. This is exactly why Ward produces balanced, compact
clusters — and why it is the same objective K-Means minimises, just optimised
greedily and bottom-up instead of iteratively.

In scikit-learn, linkage="ward" requires metric="euclidean" —
the formula above is derived from squared Euclidean distance and is meaningless
otherwise. If you need cosine or Manhattan distance, use average or
complete.
Choosing where to cut

blocks.cap:
Left: merge heights in reverse order — the largest vertical jump
marks the natural number of clusters. Middle: silhouette, exactly as for
K-Means. Right: cophenetic correlation for each linkage on the same data.

blocks.t: Three ways to pick k

1. The largest gap in merge heights. A big jump means the algorithm
was forced to join two genuinely dissimilar groups; cut just below it. This is
the dendrogram equivalent of the elbow, and it is easier to read because the
jump is a discrete event rather than a change of curvature.

2. Silhouette / other internal indices, computed on the labels from
each candidate cut. Identical machinery to Topic 76.

3. A distance threshold instead of a count. In sklearn, set
n_clusters=None and distance_threshold=t. This says "anything
closer than $t$ is the same thing" — often more meaningful than guessing a
count, especially when $t$ has physical units.

The cophenetic distance between two points is the merge height at
which they first end up in the same cluster. The cophenetic
correlation is the Pearson correlation between all cophenetic distances and
the original pairwise distances:
c = \operatorname{corr}\big({d_{\text{cophenetic}}(i,j)}, {d(i,j)}\big).

It measures how faithfully the tree preserves the true geometry. Values above
about 0.75 suggest the hierarchy is a reasonable summary; low values mean the
tree is distorting the data and you should question the linkage choice.
The cost

Hierarchical clustering does not scale. The distance matrix alone is
$O(n^2)$ memory — at $n=50{,}000$ that is 20 GB in float64. Time is
$O(n^3)$ naively, or $O(n^2\log n)$ with a priority queue; SLINK and CLINK
achieve $O(n^2)$ for single and complete linkage specifically.

Practical ceiling: around 10{,}000–30{,}000 points. Above that, either
subsample, run K-Means first and cluster the centroids hierarchically, or use
BIRCH. There is also no predict() — assigning a new point requires
rerunning the whole thing, unlike K-Means where you just find the nearest
centroid.

connectivity is the escape hatch for a specific case. Passing a
k-nearest-neighbours graph restricts merges to neighbouring points, which both
speeds things up dramatically and encodes structure (e.g. "only merge
spatially adjacent pixels" in image segmentation). It changes the result, not
just the runtime — it is a constraint, not an approximation.
Code

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import (dendrogram, linkage, fcluster,
                                     cophenet, set_link_color_palette)
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist, squareform
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph

X, y_true = make_blobs(n_samples=500, centers=5, cluster_std=1.0, random_state=11)
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE SCIPY ROUTE -- gives you the tree, which sklearn hides
# ==================================================================
Z = linkage(Xs, method="ward")     # Z is the (n-1) x 4 merge history:
# columns: [cluster_i, cluster_j, distance_at_merge, size_of_new_cluster]
print("first 3 merges:\n", Z[:3].round(3))
print("last  3 merges:\n", Z[-3:].round(3))

# Cut the tree -- two equivalent ways
labels_k = fcluster(Z, t=5,   criterion="maxclust")  # "give me exactly 5"
labels_d = fcluster(Z, t=25.0, criterion="distance") # "cut at height 25"
print("ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, labels_k), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 2. READING k OFF THE MERGE HEIGHTS -- the biggest jump
# ==================================================================
heights = Z[:, 2]
gaps    = np.diff(heights)                # increase from one merge to the next
idx     = int(np.argmax(gaps[-10:])) + len(gaps) - 10
k_suggested = len(Xs) - idx - 1
print("largest gap suggests k =", k_suggested)

for k in range(2, 9):
    lab = fcluster(Z, k, criterion="maxclust")
    print(f"k={k}  silhouette={silhouette_score(Xs, lab):.4f}")

# ==================================================================
# 3. DRAWING THE DENDROGRAM
# ==================================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
dendrogram(Z,
           ax=ax,
           truncate_mode="lastp",   # show only the last p merges
           p=20,                    # ...otherwise 500 leaves is unreadable
           show_leaf_counts=True,   # "(37)" = a collapsed subtree of 37 points
           color_threshold=Z[-4, 2],# colour below this height
           leaf_rotation=90)
ax.axhline(Z[-4, 2], color="red", linestyle="--")
ax.set_ylabel("merge distance")
# plt.savefig("dendrogram.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

# ==================================================================
# 4. COPHENETIC CORRELATION -- is the tree faithful?
# ==================================================================
D = pdist(Xs)                              # original pairwise distances
for method in ("single", "complete", "average", "ward"):
    c, _ = cophenet(linkage(Xs, method), D)
    print(f"{method:9s} cophenetic corr = {c:.4f}")
# Highest is not automatically "best" -- but a low value means the dendrogram
# is a poor summary of the actual geometry.

# ==================================================================
# 5. THE SKLEARN ROUTE -- fits the pipeline API, no tree returned
# ==================================================================
ac = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=5, linkage="ward").fit(Xs)
print("sklearn ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, ac.labels_), 3))

# Threshold instead of a count: "anything closer than 2.0 is the same thing"
ac2 = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=None, distance_threshold=2.0,
                              linkage="ward").fit(Xs)
print("threshold gave", ac2.n_clusters_, "clusters")

# Non-Euclidean metrics need a non-ward linkage
cos = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=5, metric="cosine",
                              linkage="average").fit(Xs)

# ==================================================================
# 6. CONNECTIVITY CONSTRAINTS -- only merge neighbours
# ==================================================================
# Restricts merges to the kNN graph: much faster, and encodes structure
# (spatial adjacency in images, road networks, time order in a series).
conn = kneighbors_graph(Xs, n_neighbors=10, include_self=False)
ac3 = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=5, connectivity=conn,
                              linkage="ward").fit(Xs)
print("constrained ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, ac3.labels_), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 7. THERE IS NO predict()
# ==================================================================
try:
    ac.predict(Xs[:5])
except AttributeError:
    print("AgglomerativeClustering has no predict -- assign new points by "
          "nearest centroid, or by 1-NN against the labelled training set.")

centroids = np.array([Xs[ac.labels_ == j].mean(axis=0)
                      for j in range(ac.n_clusters_)])
def assign(new):
    return np.argmin(((new[:, None, :] - centroids[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
print("assigned new points:", assign(Xs[:5]))

# ==================================================================
# 8. CLUSTERING FROM A PRECOMPUTED DISTANCE MATRIX
# ==================================================================
# Useful when your objects are not vectors (strings, graphs, users) but you
# can define a distance between them.
Dm = squareform(pdist(Xs[:200], metric="cityblock"))
ac4 = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=4, metric="precomputed",
                              linkage="average").fit(Dm)
print("precomputed labels:", np.bincount(ac4.labels_))
Everything on one page
Summary

Agglomerative: start with $n$ singleton clusters, repeatedly merge the
two closest, record every merge. Result: a dendrogram — a nested family of
clusterings at every scale.

k is chosen afterwards by cutting the tree: at a height, at a count, or
at the largest gap between consecutive merge heights.

The linkage is the real hyperparameter. Single = chains, finds
non-convex shapes, vulnerable to noise bridges. Complete = compact, equal
diameter, breaks big clusters. Average = the compromise. Ward = minimises
variance increase, behaves like K-Means, Euclidean only, and is the default.
Ward's merge cost: $\frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\|\mu_A-\mu_B\|^2$.

Cophenetic correlation tells you whether the tree faithfully
represents the original distances.

Cost: $O(n^2)$ memory, $O(n^2\log n)$ time — a hard ceiling around
$10^4$ points. Deterministic (no random seed), but there is no
predict(), and merges are greedy and irreversible.
Scale features first, exactly as for K-Means.
Interview corner
Q. What is a dendrogram and how do you read it?

A tree of the merge history. Leaves are individual points; the height of each
join is the distance at which those two clusters merged. A horizontal cut
produces a clustering, and the number of vertical lines it crosses is the number
of clusters. Tall vertical segments mean well-separated clusters.
Q. Advantage over K-Means?

You do not have to pick $k$ up front — you get every $k$ at once and choose
afterwards. It is deterministic (no seed dependence), it works with any distance
metric or a precomputed distance matrix, and the dendrogram itself is an
interpretable artefact showing structure at all scales.
Q. Disadvantage?

$O(n^2)$ memory and at least $O(n^2\log n)$ time, so it stops at around
$10^4$ points. Merges are greedy and irreversible — a bad early merge can
never be undone. And there is no predict() for new data.
Q. What is the chaining effect?

Single linkage measures cluster distance by the closest pair, so a thin bridge
of a few points joins two otherwise well-separated clusters into one long
straggly chain. It is the flip side of single linkage's ability to find
non-convex shapes.
Q. Which linkage would you choose and why?

Ward by default — compact, balanced clusters, and the objective matches
K-Means. Single if I expect elongated or curved clusters and the data is clean.
Average when I need a non-Euclidean metric such as cosine. Complete when I want
clusters with a bounded diameter.
Q. Explain Ward's linkage.

It merges the pair whose union increases total within-cluster variance least;
the increase equals $\frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\|\mu_A-\mu_B\|^2$. The size factor
penalises merging two large clusters even if their centres are close, producing
balanced results. It requires Euclidean distance.
Q. How do you pick the number of clusters from a dendrogram?

Look for the largest vertical gap between consecutive merges and cut just below
it — a big jump means the algorithm was forced to join dissimilar groups.
Confirm with silhouette across candidate cuts, and use domain knowledge.
Q. What is cophenetic correlation?

The correlation between the merge height at which two points first join and
their actual pairwise distance. It quantifies how much the tree distorts the
original geometry; a low value warns that the dendrogram is misleading.
Q. How would you cluster a million points hierarchically?

You would not, directly. Options: subsample and cluster the sample; run
MiniBatchKMeans with a few thousand centroids and cluster those
hierarchically; use BIRCH, which builds a compact CF-tree in one pass and then
clusters its summaries; or add a connectivity constraint so only neighbouring
points can ever merge.
Worked Examples
Three linkage rules on the same two clusters
One-dimensional points $x=[1,\,2,\,6,\,8]$. Agglomerative clustering merges closest pairs first.
Step 1 – first two merges. $d(1,2)=1$ is the smallest, so merge $\{1,2\}$ at height 1. Then $d(6,8)=2$, so merge $\{6,8\}$ at height 2.
Step 2 – the final merge depends on the linkage. The two remaining clusters are $\{1,2\}$ and $\{6,8\}$. Pairwise point distances are $|1-6|=5$, $|1-8|=7$, $|2-6|=4$, $|2-8|=6$.

Reading the dendrogram. Merges occur at heights $1$, $2$, then at $4$ (single), $5.5$ (average) or $7$ (complete). Cutting at height $3$ gives 2 clusters $\{1,2\}$ and $\{6,8\}$ under every rule. Cutting at height $4.5$ gives 1 cluster under single linkage (it already merged at 4) but still 2 clusters under average and complete. The same cut height means different things under different linkages.
Single linkage chains along the line (it is sensitive to noise). Complete makes compact, equal-diameter clusters. Ward (not computed here) minimises the variance increase at each merge.
